source.title: ChatGPT v Bard v Bing v Claude 2 v Aria v human-expert. How good are AI chatbots at scientific writing? (ver. 23Q3)

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream writing-task performance across chatbots and makes a limited comparison involving model size, but it does not measure pretraining loss or reproduce the original scaling-law method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a GPT-3.5 versus GPT-4 comparison of task results and parameter estimates. Its general statements about scaling and plateauing are not measurements of held-out pretraining loss, compute-optimal allocation, or fitted power laws. The cited scaling-law studies are not results of this study.
record.test_reason: This is a humanities writing evaluation of commercial chatbots. Its scale remarks (section 3.4, labelled 'a side note') compare GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Bard. Those models differ in training data, RLHF, retrieval and product design, and their sizes are estimated or assumed (Bard is assumed to be 'half' of LaMDA). Model scale is never varied in a controlled way, so the results cannot show whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or loss. The plateau conclusion is argument, not a measurement of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors call ChatGPT-4's up to 10% improvement over ChatGPT-3.5 unimpressive given an estimated tenfold parameter increase. They attribute part of it to continuous RLHF. They judge the Bard-to-GPT-4 reduction in incorrect content significant. From diminishing returns and physical limits they conclude that LLM growth has reached a plateau, citing Sam Altman.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates chatbot writing outputs rather than held-out pretraining loss across controlled model, data, or compute sweeps. The size estimates are not used in a fitted scaling-law analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The study uses two different prompts (Q1 and Q2); it reports that Q2 was especially problematic for chatbots lacking access to relevant current material. Its scaling comparison is an aggregate across the prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: GPT-4 (est. 1.8T) scores modestly higher than GPT-3.5 (175B) on an expert-graded humanities writing test. The score is -5 vs -18, but the correct-content share is lower (43% vs 46%). Fig 8 plots test performance across Bard/GPT-3.5/GPT-4 (assumed size ratio 1:2:20) as rising linearly while parameters grow exponentially. The authors attribute part of the gain to RLHF.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Across commercial chatbots with confounded training, gains on a niche expert-graded writing task look small relative to estimated parameter increases. This is not a controlled scale test.

record.problems: Only one interdisciplinary humanities case study and a limited number of human experts were used. The authors describe the tagging dataset as small and use observational analysis. The GPT-4 parameter count is an estimate, and the GPT-3.5/GPT-4 comparison does not isolate model size from other differences such as training and feedback.
record.rows_left_out: Other chatbot results are not included because their sizes are not stated or compared in a way that bears on the scale-performance relationship. The paper's parameter-growth graphic and broad plateau assertions do not provide fitted loss curves or separate model-size measurements suitable for rows.

untested.parts: No controlled scale series. The chatbot comparison confounds size with training, RLHF and retrieval, and size estimates are external or assumed.
No fitting choices or exponents are examined.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with V6 supports and limits_scope labels is overturned. The two models compared are products, not a scale series. Sizes are third-party estimates or assumptions (Bard 'half' of LaMDA). There are only two prompts, tagged by the two authors, with no uncertainty reported. Diminishing returns in absolute terms is in any case consistent with power-law scaling, so the plateau argument does not bear on V1 or V6 as stated.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss is measured against parameter count, training tokens, or compute.
No power-law fit or extrapolation from small runs is evaluated.
No fixed-compute sweep or loss-minimising parameter/token allocation is tested.
The study does not compare depth, width, or other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training regime is tested for the claimed power-law form.
The study tests a narrow humanities writing task and a limited chatbot comparison, not a general relationship across downstream tasks or performance as a function of pretraining loss.
The study does not fit scaling curves or compare fitting choices, exponents, or compute-optimal splits. Its discussion of diminishing returns does not establish departures from fitted power laws.

rows.subject: ChatGPT-3.5
rows.stage_stated: Fine-tuned from a model in the GPT-3.5 series; supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback are described.
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated chatbot answers to two one-shot scientific questions and scored quantitative accuracy.

conditions.value: Scientific writing in humanities and archaeology

rows.measure: Accuracy score, with correct and incorrect content percentages
rows.note: The paper reports these aggregate results across the two prompts.
rows.check: This is a single-chatbot score on a two-prompt humanities test, with no scale variation. As a baseline for a scale comparison it is confounded by product and training differences.

rows.subject: ChatGPT-4
rows.size_stated: Estimated at 1.8 trillion parameters; described as approximately 10 times the size of ChatGPT-3.5.
rows.stage_stated: ChatGPT-4; reinforcement learning from human feedback is described as ongoing.
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated chatbot answers to two one-shot scientific questions and scored quantitative accuracy.

conditions.value: Scientific writing in humanities and archaeology

rows.measure: Accuracy score, with correct and incorrect content percentages
rows.note: The authors say ChatGPT-4 has the highest accuracy score and that its improvement over ChatGPT-3.5 is up to 10%; the correct-content percentage itself is lower than ChatGPT-3.5's.
rows.check: GPT-4 versus GPT-3.5 confounds size (1.8T is a third-party estimate) with training, RLHF and system differences, so it does not measure a scale effect. The direction is mixed: score is -5 vs -18, but correct content is 43% vs 46%.
